patient.name: Jasmine Clarke
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then coronary care unit
patient.complaint: Central chest pain, breathlessness and palpitations, 10 days after a bad cold
background: Student nurse in Tooting; plays netball twice a week
Flu-like illness with sore throat and fever 10 days ago

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young patient, a recent flu-like illness, chest pain, a raised troponin and ECG changes that mimic MI; or 'most likely finding' (low voltage complexes, friction rub, reduced EF).

points: Jasmine, 24, has **central chest pain** like a tight band.
**Flu-like illness** with sore throat 10 days ago.
Breathless on the stairs; heart racing; very tired.
No risk factors, no drugs, no recent travel.

steps.lead: A young woman with a **viral prodrome** and chest pain: myocardial inflammation, most often **Coxsackievirus B**, mimicking MI.
Jasmine's pain, tachycardia, recent URTI and **atypical demographics for coronary disease** (young, female, no risk factors) all point to myocarditis.

visual.title: Jasmine's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia with diffuse, non-territorial ST elevation and some T wave inversion: can closely mimic STEMI. Low voltage complexes are also typical.

steps.text: The ST elevation does not fit **one artery's territory**, and there is no reciprocal depression.

steps.lead: Jasmine's ECG shows **sinus tachycardia** and **diffuse** ST elevation with T inversion: the classic STEMI mimic.

points: **Raised JVP**; an **S3 gallop**; crackles at both bases.
Soft **pericardial friction rub** at the left sternal edge.

steps.lead: Chest pain, a viral prodrome and **overt heart failure** (S3, raised JVP, hypotension): Jasmine has **fulminant myocarditis**.

steps.q: Which feature most separates Jasmine's myocarditis from a STEMI?
o: Diffuse ST elevation not in one arterial territory
steps.r: Both raise troponin and cause pain and tachycardia. **Diffuse, non-territorial** changes plus the viral history point to myocarditis.

steps.lead: Jasmine is at risk of **arrhythmia**, heart failure, **dilated cardiomyopathy** and sudden cardiac death, so she goes to the coronary care unit.

steps.text: A raised troponin with ST elevation is **not always an MI**. In a young patient after a flu-like illness, think myocarditis before sending them for PCI.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' where cardiac MRI is the gold standard (and separates myocarditis from MI), with endomyocardial biopsy for fulminant disease.

steps.lead: Jasmine's first-line tests are an **ECG** (MI-mimicking ST changes), **troponin** (raised) and an **echo** (reduced ejection fraction).

steps.title: Jasmine's bloods
steps.text: Troponin around **4000**: marked myocardial injury. Raised BNP fits heart failure.

visual.title: Jasmine's ejection fraction on echo
visual.label: Jasmine 35%
visual.caption: Global systolic dysfunction with EF as low as 35%: fulminant myocarditis, not a single-territory MI.

steps.lead: Jasmine's **cardiac MRI** shows myocardial oedema with **mid-wall/subepicardial** enhancement: the gold standard, and what separates myocarditis from MI.

steps.q: Jasmine's team want to confirm myocarditis and exclude MI without an invasive test. Which scan?
steps.r: **Cardiac MRI** is the gold standard. Its enhancement pattern separates myocarditis from MI.

steps.lead: Because Jasmine's myocarditis is **fulminant**, **endomyocardial biopsy** is the investigation of choice to confirm it and guide treatment.

visual.title: Jasmine's troponin
visual.caption: Markedly raised, falling slowly over days as the inflammation settles.

steps.title: Investigating suspected myocarditis
steps.caption: MRI distinguishes myocarditis from MI; biopsy for fulminant cases.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where the answer is supportive care, standard heart failure treatment, or exercise restriction, and PCI or thrombolysis is the classic wrong answer.

steps.lead: Jasmine's treatment is largely **supportive**: rest and continuous cardiac **monitoring** on CCU.

steps.q: Jasmine's ECG shows ST elevation. A junior suggests calling the cath lab for PCI. What do you say?
o: No: PCI has no role; this is inflammation, not occlusion
Yes: all ST elevation needs primary PCI
Yes: give thrombolysis if PCI is delayed
steps.r: **PCI has no role** in myocarditis: there is no occluded coronary artery to open.

steps.lead: Jasmine's heart failure gets standard therapy (**ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, diuretics**), arrhythmias are treated per ACLS, and she must **avoid exercise**.

steps.title: Managing Jasmine
nodes: Admit to CCU: rest and monitoring
Heart failure: ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, diuretics
steps.caption: Support the heart while the inflammation burns out.

visual.title: Jasmine's recovery
visual.caption: EF recovers on heart failure therapy. If it stayed low, she would have developed dilated cardiomyopathy.

steps.lead: Jasmine's care follows the **ESC position statement on myocarditis**: supportive care, MRI-based diagnosis and activity restriction.

steps.text: Sending a young athlete back to sport too early is dangerous: **exercise restriction** after myocarditis prevents **sudden cardiac death**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the most likely causative organism (Coxsackievirus B), why troponin rises, why MRI separates myocarditis from MI, and why exercise is restricted.

steps.lead: Jasmine's cold virus, likely **Coxsackievirus B**, invaded her cardiomyocytes; her T cells then attacked infected and bystander cells.

steps.title: From cold to heart failure
nodes: Acute heart failure; chronic: dilated cardiomyopathy

steps.lead: Jasmine's dying myocytes leaked **troponin** just as in MI, and inflammation disturbed conduction and pumping.
Jasmine's MRI enhancement is **mid-wall/subepicardial**. An MI starts at the **subendocardium** and spreads outwards (transmural).

steps.q: Which late gadolinium enhancement pattern fits Jasmine's myocarditis?
steps.r: Myocarditis: **mid-wall/subepicardial**. MI: **subendocardial/transmural** in a coronary territory.

steps.lead: Netball would raise Jasmine's myocardial workload and **arrhythmic risk** while her heart is inflamed, so exercise is restricted.

steps.text: **Inflammation, not occlusion**: myocarditis injures muscle diffusely, so ECG changes, echo dysfunction and MRI enhancement are **global or patchy**, not confined to one artery.

mcq.r: A **viral prodrome**, then chest pain mimicking MI.

o: Inferior ST elevation with reciprocal change
Sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes
mcq.r: **Sinus tachycardia**, **low voltage**, diffuse ST elevation/T inversion.
Myocyte loss can progress to **dilated cardiomyopathy**.
**Cardiac MRI**: oedema and the enhancement pattern separate it from MI.

mcq.q: Investigation of choice in fulminant myocarditis:
Why is PCI not used in myocarditis?
o: It is an inflammatory, not occlusive, process

technique.stem: A 26 year old man has 2 days of central chest pain and breathlessness. He had a flu-like illness with fever and sore throat a week ago. He has no cardiac risk factors. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 102/66 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with diffuse ST elevation that does not follow a coronary territory. Echocardiography shows globally reduced left ventricular function.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of chest pain with raised troponin in a young man.

clues: diffuse ST elevation that does not follow a coronary territory
steps.x: Viral prodrome, young, **non-territorial** changes, **global** dysfunction, markedly raised troponin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral myocardial inflammation: **myocarditis**.

elim: Pericarditis does not cause global LV dysfunction or a troponin this high.
STEMI is territorial with reciprocal change; he has no risk factors.
PE gives hypoxia and right heart strain, not diffuse ST elevation.
Takotsubo follows emotional stress, classically in older women.

steps.x: **C. Myocarditis.** Young + viral prodrome + raised troponin + global dysfunction.

technique.stem: A 22 year old woman has chest pain and palpitations 2 weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. Her troponin is raised and her ECG shows widespread T wave inversion. The team want to confirm myocarditis and distinguish it from myocardial infarction non-invasively.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic test that separates myocarditis from MI, non-invasively.

clues: 2 weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection
distinguish it from myocardial infarction non-invasively
steps.x: Suspected myocarditis; need the gold standard.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardiac MRI**: oedema and mid-wall/subepicardial enhancement.

elim: CXR cannot show myocardial inflammation.
Angiography is invasive and only excludes coronary occlusion.
CTCA shows coronary anatomy, not inflammation.
Exercise testing is dangerous in myocarditis.

steps.x: **A. Cardiac MRI.** Gold standard and the key differentiator from MI.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man is admitted with chest pain a week after a viral illness. His ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and his troponin is markedly raised. Cardiac MRI shows mid-wall enhancement. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. He is pain free and has no signs of heart failure.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Return to the gym as tolerated
Supportive care with rest and monitoring

steps.x: Initial management of confirmed myocarditis.

clues: a week after a viral illness
steps.x: MRI-confirmed myocarditis, stable, no heart failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Supportive**: rest and monitoring.

elim: No coronary disease to bypass.
PCI has no role: inflammatory, not occlusive.
Exercise must be restricted to prevent sudden death.
No thrombus to lyse.

steps.x: **D. Supportive care with rest and monitoring.** No PCI, no exercise.

technique.stem: A 28 year old woman with confirmed viral myocarditis has a cardiac MRI. A student compares it with the scan of a 64 year old man with a recent anterior myocardial infarction. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 112/72 mmHg.
technique.q: Which late gadolinium enhancement pattern is most likely on her scan?
o: Subendocardial enhancement in the LAD territory
Transmural enhancement in the LAD territory
Transmural enhancement in the RCA territory

steps.x: Which MRI pattern fits myocarditis rather than MI?
Inflammation vs ischaemic infarction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Myocarditis: **mid-wall/subepicardial**; MI starts subendocardially.

elim: Confirmed myocarditis shows enhancement and oedema.
Subendocardial in a territory is MI.
Transmural in the LAD is the man's anterior MI.
Territorial transmural enhancement is MI.

steps.x: **A. Mid-wall/subepicardial patchy enhancement.** Ischaemia hits the subendocardium first; inflammation does not.

practice.stem: A 21 year old man has 3 days of central chest pain and breathlessness. Ten days ago he had a cold with fever. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 104/68 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A young man with a recent viral illness, chest pain, tachycardia, low voltage ECG, raised troponin and reduced EF has myocarditis. Pericarditis does not reduce EF.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a young man with chest pain and raised troponin.

clues: Ten days ago he had a cold
sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes
steps.x: Young, viral prodrome, classic ECG, reduced EF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myocarditis**.

elim: Pericarditis keeps EF normal; troponin is normal or mildly raised.
HCM is familial, with an outflow murmur; no viral link.
NSTEMI is unlikely at 21 with no risk factors.
PE causes hypoxia and right strain, not reduced LV EF.

steps.x: **C. Myocarditis.** Viral prodrome + raised troponin + low voltage + reduced EF.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has 2 days of central chest pain and increasing breathlessness after a flu-like illness. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 82/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her JVP is raised and there is an S3 gallop. Echocardiography shows global systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 35%.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Central chest pain, a viral prodrome and overt heart failure (S3, raised JVP, hypotension, EF 35%) is fulminant myocarditis.

steps.x: Diagnosis: chest pain plus heart failure after a virus.
Viral prodrome + **overt heart failure** + EF 35%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fulminant myocarditis**.

elim: Pericarditis does not cause global dysfunction or shock like this.
Dissection gives tearing pain to the back, not a viral prodrome with global LV failure.
Constriction is chronic, with a normal-sized LV and preserved EF.
DCM is a chronic consequence, not a 2 day illness after a virus.

steps.x: **E. Fulminant myocarditis.** Pain + viral prodrome + overt heart failure.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has chest pain and palpitations 1 week after a sore throat and fever. His pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. His troponin is raised and echocardiography shows mildly reduced left ventricular function. His ECG is recorded.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
o: Delta waves with a short PR interval
Inferior ST elevation with reciprocal depression
Sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes
practice.e: Myocarditis typically shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes, sometimes with diffuse ST elevation and T inversion. Territorial changes with reciprocal depression suggest MI.

steps.x: ECG finding: name the diagnosis first.

clues: 1 week after a sore throat and fever
steps.x: Young, viral prodrome, myocardial injury: **myocarditis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes**.

elim: Delta waves are Wolff-Parkinson-White.
Territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change is STEMI.
Peaked T waves are hyperkalaemia.
Wellens T waves mean critical LAD stenosis.

steps.x: **D. Sinus tachycardia with low voltage complexes.**

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has chest discomfort and breathlessness 2 weeks after a flu-like illness. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. His troponin is raised and the ECG shows non-specific ST and T wave changes. Myocarditis is suspected.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
practice.e: Myocarditis often involves the pericardium too, so a pericardial friction rub may be heard. The other signs belong to coarctation, aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis and tension pneumothorax.

steps.x: Examination finding in suspected myocarditis.
The diagnosis is given; recall its signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sometimes a **pericardial friction rub**; also S3, raised JVP if fulminant.

elim: Absent femorals suggest coarctation.
Collapsing pulse is aortic regurgitation.
Ejection systolic murmur to the carotids is aortic stenosis.
Tracheal deviation suggests tension pneumothorax or collapse.

steps.x: **D. Pericardial friction rub.**

practice.stem: A 42 year old man had viral myocarditis 18 months ago and was lost to follow-up. He now has progressive breathlessness, orthopnoea and ankle swelling. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25% and normal wall thickness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic myocarditis can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy: a dilated, thin-walled, poorly contracting left ventricle with heart failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis: the long-term result of myocarditis.

clues: dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%
steps.x: Heart failure with a **dilated**, weak LV after myocarditis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dilated cardiomyopathy**, a complication of myocarditis.

elim: Constriction has a normal-sized LV with a thick pericardium.
HCM has thick walls and a small cavity.
Restrictive has stiff, non-dilated ventricles.
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic murmur, not a dilated LV.

steps.x: **B. Dilated cardiomyopathy.** Chronic myocarditis → DCM.

practice.stem: A 19 year old footballer collapses during training, 10 days after a flu-like illness. He has had palpitations for 3 days. In the ambulance his pulse rate is 190 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg. His ECG (see item resources) is shown. He has no family history of sudden death.

visual.title: Rhythm strip in the ambulance
visual.caption: Broad complex regular tachycardia at 190 bpm.

practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
practice.e: Ventricular tachycardia on exertion after a viral illness, with a markedly raised troponin and no family history, is most likely myocarditis, which causes arrhythmia and sudden death.

steps.x: The cause behind an arrhythmia in a young athlete.

clues: no family history of sudden death
steps.x: VT on exertion, viral prodrome, raised troponin, no inherited clue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myocarditis** causing VT.

elim: Brugada is inherited, with a typical V1–V2 pattern; troponin is normal.
HCM is often familial, with a murmur; troponin not this high.
Long QT is inherited and gives torsades, not a viral picture.
WPW gives delta waves and SVT.

steps.x: **D. Myocarditis.** Exercise in inflamed myocardium raises arrhythmic risk.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has chest pain a week after a viral illness. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 112/72 mmHg. Her ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and her troponin is raised. Coronary angiography is normal. The team want the gold-standard investigation to confirm the diagnosis.

practice.e: Cardiac MRI is the gold standard for myocarditis, showing oedema, hyperaemia and mid-wall/subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement.

steps.x: MI excluded; need to prove myocardial inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardiac MRI**.

elim: CTCA shows arteries, already normal.
Exercise is dangerous in myocarditis.
Repeating angiography adds nothing.
A throat swab does not confirm myocardial disease.

practice.stem: A 32 year old man is in the coronary care unit with suspected myocarditis after a flu-like illness. He has worsening breathlessness. steps.x: Investigation of choice: decide if this is fulminant.
Shock and overt heart failure: **fulminant** myocarditis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

Dual antiplatelets are ACS treatment.

practice.stem: A 20 year old semi-professional footballer is recovering from myocarditis diagnosed 2 weeks ago. He feels well and wants to return to training this weekend. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. His troponin is still mildly raised.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Return to sport if the ECG is normal
practice.e: Exercise raises myocardial workload and arrhythmic risk in inflamed myocardium. Activity restriction helps prevent sudden cardiac death.

steps.x: Advice after myocarditis in an athlete.
Recent myocarditis, ongoing injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Restrict exercise** to prevent sudden cardiac death.

elim: Any training raises arrhythmic risk now.
Feeling well does not mean the myocardium has healed.
A normal ECG does not exclude ongoing inflammation.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has chest pain and a markedly raised troponin 10 days after a febrile illness with sore throat and diarrhoea. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg. Cardiac MRI confirms myocarditis. Her friend from the same university halls had a similar viral illness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Coxsackievirus B, a cardiotropic enterovirus spread in close communities, is the most common cause of viral myocarditis.

steps.x: Organism question for viral myocarditis.

clues: febrile illness with sore throat and diarrhoea
steps.x: Enteroviral-type illness spreading in halls, then myocarditis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coxsackievirus B** (enterovirus).

elim: CMV myocarditis is mostly in the immunocompromised.
EBV causes glandular fever; rarely myocarditis.
HSV is not a classic cardiotropic virus.
Strep pyogenes causes rheumatic fever weeks after tonsillitis.

steps.x: **A. Coxsackievirus B.** The commonest cause of myocarditis.

glossary.Myocarditis: Inflammation of the heart muscle, usually viral, that can mimic a heart attack.
glossary.Myocardium: The muscular middle layer of the heart wall.
glossary.Coxsackievirus B: Enterovirus that is the most common cause of viral myocarditis.
glossary.Enterovirus: Group of viruses including Coxsackie, spread by the faecal-oral and respiratory routes.
glossary.Cardiotropic: Having a tendency to infect heart tissue.
glossary.Viral prodrome: The early flu-like symptoms of a viral infection before the main illness.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, such as a cold or sore throat.
glossary.Fulminant myocarditis: Severe, rapidly progressive myocarditis with overt heart failure or shock.
glossary.S3 gallop: Third heart sound in early diastole, a sign of a failing, overfilled ventricle.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure; raised in heart failure and fluid overload.
glossary.Ejection fraction: Percentage of blood pumped out of the left ventricle with each beat; normal is over 50%.
glossary.EF: Ejection fraction: the proportion of ventricular blood ejected per beat.
glossary.Global systolic dysfunction: The whole ventricle contracts poorly, not just one coronary territory.
glossary.Low voltage complexes: Small QRS complexes on the ECG, seen with myocardial oedema or effusion.
glossary.Pericardial friction rub: Scratching sound heard when inflamed pericardial layers rub together.
glossary.Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium causing pleuritic chest pain and saddle ST elevation.
glossary.Myopericarditis: Inflammation affecting both the myocardium and the pericardium.
glossary.Troponin: Heart muscle protein released when myocytes are damaged; raised in MI and myocarditis.
glossary.Cardiac MRI: Magnetic resonance scan of the heart; the gold-standard test for myocarditis.
glossary.Late gadolinium enhancement: Bright areas on cardiac MRI after contrast showing scar or inflammation.
glossary.LGE: Late gadolinium enhancement: MRI marker of scar or inflammation in the myocardium.
glossary.Subepicardial: The outer layer of the myocardium, just under the epicardium.
glossary.Subendocardial: The inner layer of the myocardium; where ischaemic damage starts in MI.
glossary.Transmural: Through the full thickness of the heart wall.
glossary.Endomyocardial biopsy: Sample of heart muscle taken via a catheter; investigation of choice in fulminant myocarditis.
glossary.Dilated cardiomyopathy: Enlarged, weak left ventricle with poor pumping; a chronic result of myocarditis.
glossary.DCM: Dilated cardiomyopathy: dilated, poorly contracting ventricle causing heart failure.
glossary.Sudden cardiac death: Unexpected death from a cardiac cause, usually an arrhythmia.
glossary.ACLS: Advanced cardiac life support: the standard algorithms for treating cardiac arrest and arrhythmias.
glossary.CCU: Coronary care unit: ward with continuous cardiac monitoring.
glossary.Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: Stress-induced apical ballooning of the left ventricle, mimicking MI.
glossary.NT-proBNP: Hormone released by stretched ventricles; raised in heart failure.
glossary.PCI: Percutaneous coronary intervention; has no role in myocarditis as no artery is blocked.
glossary.Ventricular tachycardia: Fast broad-complex rhythm from the ventricles; can cause collapse or sudden death.
